g1: Picture pulling an empty cart and a loaded cart with the same net force. Which one gains speed faster?
g2: Choose a slide lead and a scribe. Everyone predicts first and saves their own reasoning.
g3: Agree on who handles the equipment, checks safety, records readings, and checks the math. Share results after everyone has a job.
g4: Level the track first. Connect the cart and sensor, then set up the string and pulley. Leave space for the hanging mass to fall safely.
g5: Try a short release. Check that velocity rises smoothly before recording a trial. If the trace looks wrong, fix the setup first.
g6: Change the moving mass. Keep the pulling setup steady. Use the change in velocity each second to compare trials.
g7: A small push can act for a long time. Keep the force, mass, and time separate when you explain the asteroid story.
g8: Read the position axis first. Follow the line to find how far position drops in each second. Use the sign to give direction.
g9: Yesterday you named forces. Today you will compare how much the same net force changes the motion of different masses.
g10: Compare two bars. Read their mass labels before comparing their heights. The bars show a prediction to test.
g11: Imagine sharing the same pull across more moving mass. Make a prediction before opening the answer.
g12: Move the same time step along both lines. The line with the bigger velocity gain has the greater acceleration.
g13: Use the same hanger for each run. Add mass to the cart, then record what changed and what stayed fixed.
g14: Draw a boundary around everything that speeds up together. Include the cart, its added load, and the hanger when finding total moving mass.
g15: The hanger’s weight pulls the whole system. A fixed hanger keeps that driving force steady, but friction can still affect the result.
g16: Name one thing you change, one thing you measure, and two things you keep the same. Explain why one control matters.
g17: Keep each trial in a separate row. Write the mass, its unit, and the slope of the velocity graph before comparing runs.
g18: Repeat the release from the same mark without pushing. A repeat tells you how much the readings vary for one mass.
g19: Choose a straight part of the velocity trace while the hanger is falling. Leave out the push, catch, and bounce.
g20: If both mass and pull change, either change could affect the slope. Decide what to restore for a fair test.
g21: Point to two rows from the same data source. Read the values aloud before making a claim about the pattern.
g22: Multiply mass by acceleration for two runs. Similar products support a nearly steady net force. Look for a reason the products might differ.
g23: Keep the push the same and picture a larger asteroid. Think about how acting earlier could change where it ends up.
g24: Write raw readings with units before finding a mean. Label whether each row came from your cart or from supplied data.
g25: Pick two points on a straight section. Subtract the velocities and divide by the time between the points.
g26: Use the final reading minus the first reading in both the top and bottom of your slope calculation. Keep the units.
g27: Compare the ratio of the masses with the ratio of the accelerations. Say whether the change agrees with your prediction.
g28: These numbers come from a calculation. Use them if needed, name their source, and keep them separate from measurements.
g29: State the pattern using two values. If a trial breaks the pattern, describe it and suggest a check.
g30: Work alone. Say whether you doubled the cart alone or the whole moving mass. Use total moving mass when applying the rule.
b1: Point to the whiteboard. The group changes cart mass and keeps the hanger fixed. Name one other control that makes two runs fair to compare.
alt1: Students list what to change, measure, and keep the same.
b2: The notebook reports film sample data for cart mass and acceleration. Read one row with units. Say how the graph’s slope could give the acceleration.
alt2: Film sample table with four cart masses and accelerations.
b3: The film table uses cart mass. Multiplying it by acceleration estimates net force on the cart. In the deck’s whole-system model, use total moving mass instead.
alt3: Cart mass times acceleration gives nearly the same force in each film row.
t4: Give a push time to act
b4: Under the same net force, more mass means less acceleration. A small acceleration can still change velocity if it lasts long enough.
alt4: The notebook compares acceleration at the same force as mass increases.
q1: Which change tests the effect of mass while keeping the driving setup steady?
o1: Add weight to the cart and keep the hanger fixed.
o2: Increase the hanger mass with every run.
o3: Tip the track more each time.
q2: Predict how acceleration changes if total moving mass doubles at the same net force. Explain which masses you count.
q3: For each mass you tested, record total moving mass in kg and each trial’s acceleration in m/s². Keep failed releases marked. If using supplied data, name the source, record two rows with units, and explain one limit.
q4: Use two velocity and time readings to calculate acceleration. Show the changes you divided, the unit, and where the readings came from. You may use the clean trial on the slides.
q5: Use two rows from the same source to test your prediction. Compare mass times acceleration and explain one reason a real trial might differ from the ideal model.
q6: The same net force acts on two systems. One system has twice the total moving mass. Predict its acceleration compared with the other. Would doubling only the cart always give the same result? Explain.
a2: At fixed net force, doubling total moving mass halves acceleration. The moving mass includes cart, load, and hanger.
a4: Divide the change in velocity by elapsed time. In the supplied clean trial, (0.40 − 0.10) / (0.80 − 0.20) gives 0.50 m/s².
a6: Acceleration halves only when total moving mass doubles at fixed net force. A fixed hanger still contributes to total mass.
p1a: Sketch the moving system. Mark where you add mass and what stays fixed.
p1b: Draw two velocity lines for the same net force. Predict which mass gives the steeper line.
p2a: Share two mass and acceleration rows. Name your source, units, and what mass your rows represent.
p2b: Check how the slope was found. Explain what could make one trial unreliable.
p3a: Use two products of mass and acceleration to defend or revise your prediction.
p3b: Use the same-force rule for an asteroid. Explain one limit of carrying the cart result over to space.
discuss: Switch roles at the whiteboard. Compare one mass, slope, or assumption in each other’s explanation.
reply: Point to one value or line your classmate used. Explain what it supports or what needs a second look.
reflect: State one part of your explanation you checked or changed and why.
ex1: Adding mass to both the cart and hanger makes a fair test of mass alone.
ex2: A high point on the velocity graph always means large acceleration.
ex3: A heavy asteroid cannot change velocity, even if a net force acts for a long time.
crit: Check the claim using a mass, a graph, or a trial. Give a corrected explanation.
sample: Use the slide’s ideal model table if you have no equipment. The clean trial on the slides also provides two time and velocity readings for slope. Label each source. Never report supplied values as your measurements.
solo: Work on your own. Give your prediction, critique the sample claim, and save your final reasoning.
